extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying patent amendment doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing disclaimers and re-issue (amendment) of patents: when disclaimers affect costs or are nullities, statutory preconditions for re-issue, what defects re-issue may cure, and limits (delay, fraud, breadth changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer prerequisite for recovery of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: That the plaintiff, where he is entitled to recover under that section, shall not recover costs unless he has entered a disclaimer, prior to the commencement of the suit, of what he claimed without right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclaimer was entered in the Patent Office before the suit was instituted, the plaintiff recovers costs in the usual way (independently of any question of disclaimer). If the disclaimer is entered after suit commencement (during the progress of the trial) plaintiff may recover on the merits but will not be entitled to costs. See Hall v. Wiles and Guyon v. Serrell examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of filing disclaimer during suit
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer being filed during suit, the plaintiff can recover no costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple authorities: Hayes v. Bickelhoupt; Buidett v. Estey. Filing during suit may save the suit on the merits but forfeits costs unless other conditions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing disclaimer before suit affects only costs absent unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: That the filing of a disclaimer before suit affects only the costs, if there is no question of unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclaimer is timely (before suit) it governs costs but does not otherwise change substantive rights; however, an unreasonable delay in filing can raise separate issues (see cases cited like Dunbar v. Myers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer is a nullity unless there is real excess or necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer filed without sufficient cause is a nullity under this as well as the former section of the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no real excess of claim according to judicial construction, a disclaimer pending suit does not admit inability to recover costs. A disclaimer of something not claimed in the patent is also a nullity. Cases: Sharp v. Tifft; Tuck v. Bramhill; other cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer of matter not claimed is void
rubrics_metrics.description: That a disclaimer of a part or act not claimed in the patent is a nullity; a disclaimer of something not claimed in the patent is a nullity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such disclaimers have no operative effect either as amendment or upon costs. See Sharp v. Tifft and related citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where disclaimer pending suit does not prejudice defendant, proceedings need not be recommenced
rubrics_metrics.description: That where a disclaimer was made pending suit, and the defendant was not prejudiced thereby, the proceedings need not be recommenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclaimer cures the issue and defendant's interests are not harmed, courts may proceed without restarting litigation. See Libbey v. Mt. Washington Glass Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery on valid claims despite failure to disclaim
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patentee can recover on the valid claims, notwithstanding his failure to disclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file a disclaimer does not necessarily bar recovery on claims that are valid and truly his; costs and other consequences may still be affected. See Kittle v. Hall (1887).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue permitted only for errors from inadvertence, accident, or mistake (no fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent might be surrendered and re-issued if the error had arisen from inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without any fraudulent or deceptive intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core statutory precondition for re-issue (act of 1832 and repeated in later acts). Re-issue privilege was introduced to correct patents invalid or inoperative for such non-fraudulent defects. Authorities and legislative history emphasize the no-fraud requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory obligations under early acts (oath, full written description, drawings/models)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligations imposed upon the patentee by the third section of the act of 1793 were: (1) To make oath that he believed himself to be the true inventor; (2) To deliver a written description of his invention in such complete and exact language as to distinguish it from all other things before known and enable any person skilled in the art to construct and use it; (3) To furnish drawings, model, or specimens as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure in these obligations (except where explained by inadvertence/accident/mistake) made a patent invalid or inoperative and justified re-issue to cure defects in disclosure or identification of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (enablement and distinctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description must be so full, clear, and exact as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, and to distinguish the invention from all other things before known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defects in the description fall into two classes: (1) defects in disclosure to the public (enablement); (2) defects in defining precise limits (distinguishing from prior art). Re-issue mainly cures these defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between description and specification/claim (act of 1836)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of 1836 prescribed that the inventor should 'particularly specify and point out that which he claimed to be his own invention or discovery' — establishing the Claim (specification) as distinct from the Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is central for re-issue law: 'description' = detailed delineation for public use; 'specification' (or 'claim') = the specific statement of what is claimed. Re-issues relate differently to defects in each part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for re-issue (defective/insufficient description or excessive claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issues were limited to cases where a patent was 'inoperative or invalid, by reason of a defective or insufficient description or specification, or by reason of the patentee claiming in his specification, as his own invention, more than he had, or shall have, a right to claim as new.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principal grounds: curing defective/insufficient disclosure (description/specification) and correcting an excessive claim. Historically courts have differed about whether re-issue can enlarge claims; modern view: enlargements only when actual inadvertent mistake exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot be used to broaden claims except for bona fide mistake; delay may bar re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue for the purpose of enlarging and expanding the Claim of a patent was not comprised within the literal terms of the law except where an actual mistake had occurred; an unreasonable delay in applying for a re-issue indicates the allegation of inadvertence or mistake is a mere pretence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issues for claim enlargement should be exception, not rule. Courts condemn using re-issue to capture later developments (waiting until others make improvements and then expanding). Miller v. Brass Co. and related commentary stress bona fide inadvertence as necessary and warn against abuse due to delay or sleeping on rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requisites for obtaining a re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner shall, on the surrender of such patent, and the payment of the duty required by law, cause a new patent, for the same invention, and in accordance with the corrected specification, to be issued to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender, payment of duty, and corrected specification are formal preconditions. The re-issued patent is to be for the same invention with corrected description/specification per statutory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court will protect defendants' interests on post-commencement disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: That under the act of 1887 a disclaimer may be filed after the commencement of a suit, and the court will duly protect the interests of the defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While post-commencement disclaimers generally affect costs or may be nullities if unnecessary, courts have authority to protect defendants and preserve fairness (e.g., Smith v. Nichols). Whether proceedings must be recommenced depends on prejudice to defendant.
